summary: A 1970 note proposing a language-machine for data reconfiguration, by three RAND authors. It deals with converting data from one arrangement to another so different systems can share it.

eli5.summary: A way to rearrange information from the shape one computer likes to the shape another computer likes.

questions: how do different computers exchange data
how did early networks handle format differences
subtitle: A language for converting data formats between different computers

tldr.problem: Different computers store and represent data in incompatible ways, making it difficult for systems on the ARPANET to share files and databases.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 83 proposes a Form Machine: a syntax-driven interpreter that applies a set of grammar rules (replacement rules) to transform input data from one format to another. Rules are ordered by priority; the machine applies rules sequentially until matching one transforms the input.
tldr.outcome: This approach simplifies the Protocol Manager by standardizing how two systems negotiate their data formats using a small set of pre-specified forms, rather than building custom converters for each pair.

facts.label: Authors
facts.value: R. Anderson, A. Harslem, J. Heafner (RAND)

facts.label: Data types supported
facts.value: Decimal, octal, hex, ASCII, EBCDIC, binary

today: RFC 83 proposed a data transformation language for ARPANET, but is now obsolete in practice. Modern systems use standardized formats (JSON, XML, Protocol Buffers) and serialization libraries rather than custom grammar-based rules. However, the idea of declarative format conversion rules influenced later data integration tools.

sections.title: The Data Conversion Problem
sections.content: RFC 83, authored by Anderson, Harslem, and Heafner at RAND, proposes a solution to data reconfiguration. When a RAND console needs to talk to UCLA's remote job system on an IBM 360/91, data must be converted between formats. Rather than building a new converter for each system pair, the authors propose a reusable machine that interprets grammar-based replacement rules.
sections.eli5: When different computers need to send data to each other, one computer's format doesn't match the other's. A translator needs rules for how to convert.

sections.title: The Form Machine
sections.content: A form is an ordered set of rules. Each rule is a replacement operation: a pattern on the left-hand side matches input data, and the right-hand side specifies what output to emit. Rules are tried in priority order; if a rule fails, the next one is tried. A term in a rule describes data to match or emit, with fields for name, data type (like decimal, octal, hex, ASCII, EBCDIC, or binary), replication, value, and length. The machine is not a general programming language but a specialized tool for format conversion.
sections.eli5: Rules describe patterns like 'if you see this, turn it into that'. The machine tries rules one by one until one works, then starts over with higher-priority rules.

sections.title: Real-World Use
sections.content: The RFC includes examples of data reconfigurations needed between RAND and UCLA. The simplicity of the Form Machine means a few pre-defined forms can handle conversation between two systems: one system sends data in its natural format, the Form Machine converts it to the other system's format, and vice versa. This reduces the complexity of the Protocol Manager, which no longer needs custom converters for every system pair.
sections.eli5: A RAND computer sends its data in RAND format, the translator machine converts it to UCLA format, and UCLA reads it normally.
